Amazon Aurora
• 	Aurora is a proprietary technology from AWS (not open sourced)
• 	Postgres and MySQL are both supported as Aurora DB (that means your
drivers will work as if Aurora was a Postgres or MySQL database)
• 	Aurora is “AWS cloud optimized” and claims 5x performance improvement
over MySQL on RDS, over 3x the performance of Postgres on RDS
• 	Aurora storage automatically grows in increments of 10GB, up to 256 TB.
• 	Aurora can have up to 15 replicas and the replication process is faster than
MySQL (sub 10 ms 	replica lag)
• 	Failover in Aurora is instantaneous. It’s HA (High Availability) native.
• 	Aurora costs more than RDS (20% more) – but is more efficient
© Stephane Maarek

• 	At-rest encryption:
• 	Database master & replicas encryption using AWS KMS – must be defined as launch time

## Database failover versus read scaling

A traditional RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment provides a standby for availability; read replicas offload reads with replication lag. Check the specific RDS or Aurora deployment type rather than assuming every standby is readable.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

Multi-AZ is the availability feature that matches the failure requirement. Backups address restoration rather than immediate managed failover, while caching is not a replacement for an authoritative database. Client reconnection and DNS behavior still matter.

### Avoid this trap

A read replica is not automatically the same as managed synchronous failover. RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters and Aurora have different readable-instance capabilities from a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance.

### Apply it

A production relational database needs managed failover after an AZ failure. The primary bottleneck is not read throughput. Which change most directly addresses the need?

**Recommended design:** Enable an appropriate Multi-AZ deployment and test application reconnect behavior.

Multi-AZ is the availability feature that matches the failure requirement. Backups address restoration rather than immediate managed failover, while caching is not a replacement for an authoritative database. Client reconnection and DNS behavior still matter.

cards.question: What is traditional RDS Multi-AZ primarily for?
cards.answer: Availability through managed failover to a standby.

cards.question: What is a read replica primarily for?

quiz.question: A production relational database needs managed failover after an AZ failure. The primary bottleneck is not read throughput. Which change most directly addresses the need?
options: Create an asynchronous read replica and assume it automatically replaces all failover handling.
Add ElastiCache as the authoritative copy of all database records.
Enable an appropriate Multi-AZ deployment and test application reconnect behavior.
Increase the backup retention period without changing the deployment topology.

## Caching and stale data

A cache reduces repeated database reads and latency when the access pattern has reusable data. Design expiration, invalidation and miss behavior explicitly; the database remains authoritative unless the application deliberately chooses another model.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

Cache-aside fits repeated reads with bounded staleness. TTL and invalidation control freshness; fallback and stampede controls protect the database. Multi-AZ is an availability design, not a guarantee that a query becomes faster.

### Avoid this trap

A cache can return stale values and can experience a surge of misses after eviction or failure. It does not make a write-heavy transaction workload disappear.

### Apply it

A product catalog repeats the same reads thousands of times per second and tolerates values that are briefly stale. How should the architect reduce database load?

**Recommended design:** Use cache-aside with ElastiCache, a suitable TTL and a controlled database fallback.
